entry: Small eight-legged [[Arthropod|arthropod]] of the class Arachnida, found in virtually every terrestrial and aquatic ecosystem. Mites belong to two large orders, the Acariformes and Parasitiformes, and about 48,000 species have been described. Most are less than 1 mm (0.04 in) long and have a simple, unsegmented body plan. Mites act as decomposers, predators and plant feeders, and some are parasites, including the Varroa parasite of [[Honey bee|honey bees]] and the scabies mites of humans. Most species are harmless to people, but a few cause allergies or transmit diseases, and many mites and ticks transmit pathogens that cause diseases such as [[Lyme disease]]. Genetic studies have questioned whether mites form a natural group, since Parasitiformes may be more closely related to other chelicerates than to Acariformes. The study of mites is called acarology.

Hellenistic king of Pontus (r. 120–63 BC) and a leading opponent of the Roman Republic. He came to the throne as a teenager after his father's assassination, under the regency of his mother, Laodice VI, whom he overthrew in 113 BC. He extended Pontus around the [[Black Sea]] and into Asia Minor, which led to conflict with Rome. In 89 BC he overran Roman Asia, ordering massacres of Romans and Italians, and brought much of mainland Greece, including [[Athens]], to his side. [[Sulla]] defeated his forces in the First Mithridatic War, and further wars followed. After a defeat by [[Pompey]] at the Battle of the Lycus in 66 BC, Mithridates fled to [[Crimea]], where his son Pharnaces rebelled against him, and he committed suicide.

Organelle found in most eukaryotic cells, where it carries out aerobic respiration. Mitochondria have a double membrane and generate [[Adenosine triphosphate|adenosine triphosphate]] (ATP), the chemical energy used throughout the cell. Their compartments include the outer membrane, intermembrane space, inner membrane, cristae (infoldings that increase surface area) and matrix. Mitochondria also take part in signaling, cell differentiation, cell death and control of the cell cycle. The number per cell varies widely: a mature red blood cell has none, while a liver cell can have more than 2,000. Mitochondria have their own genome, similar to bacterial genomes, which supports the [[Symbiogenesis|endosymbiotic]] origin of the organelle from free-living prokaryotes. Mitochondrial diseases, [[Heart failure|heart failure]] and autism are among the conditions in which mitochondria are implicated.

Process of cell division in eukaryotes in which replicated [[Chromosome|chromosomes]] separate into two new nuclei, producing two genetically identical daughter cells. Mitosis is part of the [[Cell cycle|cell cycle]] and follows the S phase of interphase, when DNA is replicated. Through the stages of prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase, the duplicated chromosomes condense and attach to spindle fibers that pull one copy of each to opposite sides of the cell, and cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm. Animal cells usually undergo open mitosis, in which the nuclear envelope breaks down, whereas fungal cells generally undergo closed mitosis. Errors can produce three or more daughter cells, cause mutations or trigger apoptosis, and some [[Cancer|cancers]] arise from such mutations. Prokaryotes, which lack a true nucleus, divide by binary fission instead.

American businessman and former politician, [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] nominee in the 2012 presidential election. Romney co-founded the private equity firm Bain Capital in 1984. He served as governor of [[Massachusetts]] from 2003 to 2007 and as a senator from [[Utah]] from 2019 to 2025. In the 2012 election he lost to [[Barack Obama]]. As a senator he voted to convict [[Donald Trump]] at his first impeachment trial, the first time a senator had voted to convict a president of his own party in such a trial.

Full-contact combat sport based on striking and grappling, combining techniques from various combat sports. Its precursors include unrestricted contests in East Asia and Brazil's vale tudo bouts, which drew on [[Judo]], [[Brazilian jiu-jitsu]] and [[Muay Thai]]. A 1976 exhibition in Japan between [[Muhammad Ali]] and Antonio Inoki was another early mixed bout. Brazilian jiu-jitsu was brought to the United States, and the [[Ultimate Fighting Championship|UFC]] was founded in 1993 with almost no rules. The term mixed martial arts first appeared in a 1993 review of UFC 1. Safety rules were added over time to meet sport regulations and win mainstream acceptance. By the early 2000s the sport had become a global phenomenon, rivaling [[Boxing|boxing]] and [[Professional wrestling|professional wrestling]] in pay-per-view business.

Material made of two or more substances combined physically, without chemical bonding. Each constituent keeps its own chemical identity and properties, so a mixture can usually be separated by physical methods such as [[Filtration|filtration]], [[Distillation|distillation]] or evaporation. Its physical properties, such as melting point, may differ from those of its components. Homogeneous mixtures, or [[Solution (chemistry)|solutions]], are uniform throughout, as with air and saltwater. Heterogeneous mixtures have visible or detectable phases, as with sand in water and oil-and-vinegar dressing, an [[Emulsion|emulsion]]. Azeotropes are mixtures that are especially difficult to separate, and mixtures may take the form of solutions, suspensions or colloids. Most matter encountered in everyday life is a mixture.

Japanese swordsman, strategist, writer, artist and rōnin. He was renowned for his undefeated record in 62 duels, many fought with a sword in each hand. He founded the Niten Ichi-ryū school of swordsmanship, which used a [[Katana|katana]] and a wakizashi together. He is believed to have fought at the [[Battle of Sekigahara|Battle of Sekigahara]], the Siege of Osaka and the Shimabara Rebellion. Late in life he wrote *The Book of Five Rings* (*Go Rin No Sho*), a treatise on strategy divided into five elements, and *Dokkōdō* (*The Path of Aloneness*), a set of 21 precepts. He left both to his student Terao Magonojō shortly before his death. Musashi also produced ink paintings and [[Calligraphy|calligraphy]] in a [[Zen|Zen]]-influenced style, including a [[Shrike|shrike]] on a dead branch that symbolized resilience.

State in northeastern India, bordered by [[Bangladesh|Bangladesh]] and [[Myanmar|Myanmar]]. Aizawl is the capital and largest city. Mizoram is predominantly [[Christianity|Christian]], with about 87% of the population practicing Christianity. Mizo is the most widely spoken language and, with English, its official language. About 84.53% of the state is forested. After an uprising that began in 1966, the 1986 Mizoram Peace Accord paved the way for statehood on 20 February 1987, as India's 23rd state.

Extinct order of flightless birds (Dinornithiformes) endemic to [[New Zealand]]. The nine species, in six genera, were the largest terrestrial animals and dominant [[Herbivore|herbivores]] in New Zealand's forests until the arrival of the Māori, and the two largest stood about 3.6 meters (12 ft) tall. Unlike other ratites, moa lacked even vestigial wings. Genetic studies place their closest living relatives among the flighted [[Tinamou|tinamous]] of South America. Fossil evidence shows they diversified during the Pleistocene and thrived in isolation until human arrival. Moa were hunted only by [[Haast's eagle]], but Polynesian settlers hunted them intensively for food, and they were driven to [[Extinction|extinction]] primarily through overhunting.

Monolithic human figures carved by the Rapa Nui people on [[Easter Island]] in [[Polynesia|eastern Polynesia]] between about 1250 and 1500. Hundreds were carved from volcanic stone at the Rano Raraku quarry, and many were moved to coastal stone platforms called ahu, where they faced inland toward clan lands. The moai are considered the living faces of deified ancestors. The tallest erected, Paro, was almost 10 meters (33 ft) high and weighed 82 metric tons. The statues were moved without wheels or draft animals. Europeans first visited in 1722 and found the statues still gazing inland, but many were toppled in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, possibly because of European contact or tribal warfare.

Deep, broad ditch dug around a [[Castle|castle]], fortification or town, either dry or filled with water. Moats gave a site a preliminary line of defense, especially against siege engines. They usually denied direct access except at a few narrow points crossed by drawbridges, [[Bridge|bridges]] or causeways, where a [[Siege|siege]] could be funneled and more easily defended. Moats could be expanded into more extensive water defenses, including lakes, [[Dam|dams]] and sluices. They appeared in fortifications from ancient Egypt to medieval Europe, [[Angkor Wat]] and colonial forts in the Americas. The development of gunpowder [[Artillery|artillery]] made static water barriers less effective, and later moats were often ornamental.

Port city and county seat of Mobile County, Alabama (pop., 2020: 187,041). Alabama's only deep-water port, Mobile lies on the Mobile River at the head of Mobile Bay on the Gulf Coast. French colonists settled the site in 1702, and its port has long been central to the local economy. Mobile surrendered to Union forces in April 1865, during the [[American Civil War]], after Union victories at two forts protecting the city. The city is known for [[Mardi Gras|Mardi Gras]], the oldest organized Carnival celebration in the United States, which dates from the first decade of the 18th century.

Software application designed to run on mobile devices such as smartphones and tablets. Apps were originally intended for productivity tasks such as email and calendars, but have expanded into games, location services and ticketing. Native apps are designed for a specific operating system, typically [[IOS|iOS]] or [[Android (operating system)|Android]]. Web apps run through a [[Web browser|browser]], while hybrid apps use web technologies inside a native container. Apps are generally downloaded from app stores, a type of digital distribution platform.

Computer small enough to hold and operate in the hand. Mobile devices are typically battery-powered and have a flat-panel display and one or more built-in input devices, such as a [[Touchscreen|touchscreen]] or keypad. They include smartphones, tablets and wearables such as smartwatches. Modern devices emphasize wireless networking to the [[Internet|Internet]] and to nearby devices through [[Wi-Fi|Wi-Fi]], [[Bluetooth|Bluetooth]], cellular networks or near-field communication. Their origins lie in cellular telephones and personal digital assistants of the 1980s. Excessive use has been associated with anxiety, depression and musculoskeletal strain, and pervasive data collection raises privacy concerns. Large-scale reviews find limited causal evidence for severe health risks from typical radiation exposure.

Congolese military officer and president of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zaire (r. 1965–97). He deposed the elected government of [[Patrice Lumumba|Patrice Lumumba]] in 1960 and seized power directly in a 1965 coup. He founded the Popular Movement of the Revolution as the sole legal party in 1967 and renamed the country Zaire in 1971. His program of "national authenticity" sought to erase colonial cultural influence, but his regime was marked by human rights abuses and a [[Cult of personality|cult of personality]]. As an opponent of [[Communism|communism]], he received strong support from the United States, France and Belgium. His rule has been called a kleptocracy, and estimates of his personal wealth range from $50 million to $5 billion. Economic collapse forced him to accept multiparty politics in 1990. In 1997 rebels led by Laurent-Désiré Kabila drove him into exile in Morocco, where he died of prostate cancer.

Epic novel by American writer [[Herman Melville|Herman Melville]], published in 1851. Its narrator, the sailor Ishmael, joins the whaling ship *Pequod*, whose captain, Ahab, seeks vengeance on the white [[Sperm whale|sperm whale]] Moby Dick, which had bitten off his leg. Melville drew on his years as a common sailor and on [[Whaling|whaling]] literature, and the ending is based on the sinking of the whaleship *Essex* in 1820. The novel received mixed reviews and was a commercial failure, and it was out of print when Melville died. Its reputation as a Great American Novel was established only in the 20th century. [[William Faulkner|William Faulkner]] said he wished he had written it himself.

Pre-Columbian civilization that flourished on the northern coast of [[Peru|Peru]] from about AD 100 to 800. Many scholars contend that the Moche were not a monolithic empire but a group of autonomous polities sharing a common culture, evident in their iconography and monumental architecture. They built irrigation systems from rivers to support intensive agriculture, and constructed platform mounds called huacas, such as the Huaca del Sol and Huaca de la Luna near present-day Trujillo. Elite tombs, such as those of the Lords of Sipán, contained gold, silver and turquoise artifacts. Moche ceramics depicted portraits, daily life and warfare, and religious practice included [[Human sacrifice|human sacrifice]] of combatants. The culture declined around AD 800, possibly as a result of climatic disruption such as prolonged El Niño events.

Family of [[New World|New World]] [[Passerine|passerine]] birds known for vocal mimicry. Mockingbirds, of which there are about 35 species including thrashers and catbirds, imitate the songs of other birds as well as insects, amphibians and even car alarms. Males may have lifetime repertoires exceeding 200 phrases and often sing late at night. The northern mockingbird, the most widespread species in North America, is an opportunistic omnivore. Pairs are typically monogamous and defend their territory aggressively when raising young. In 1927 [[Texas|Texas]] became the first state to choose a state bird, and [[Arkansas|Arkansas]], [[Florida|Florida]], [[Mississippi|Mississippi]] and [[Tennessee|Tennessee]] later adopted the northern mockingbird as well.

Ninth emperor of the [[Aztec Empire|Aztec Empire]] (r. 1502–1520). During his reign the empire reached its greatest size, expanding through warfare as far south as Xoconosco in Chiapas and the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, and incorporating the Zapotec and Yopi peoples. He widened the divide between nobles and commoners by barring commoners from working in royal palaces. His reign saw the first contact between [[Mesoamerica|Mesoamerican]] and European civilizations. He died early in the [[Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire|Spanish conquest]], as [[Hernán Cortés|Hernán Cortés]] and his men seized [[Tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]], and the circumstances of his death remain disputed. Spanish accounts describe him as weak-willed and indecisive, but contemporary depictions of him are divided.

Fifth tlatoani of [[Tenochtitlan|Tenochtitlan]] and second Aztec emperor (r. 1440–1469). During his reign the Aztec Empire was consolidated and expanded, and Tenochtitlan became the dominant partner in the Aztec Triple Alliance. His military campaigns extended Aztec influence south to [[Oaxaca|Oaxaca]] in 1445 and against the Mixteca peoples. With Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco he built the Chapultepec aqueduct, completed around 1466, which supplied fresh water to the growing city. He enacted sixteen known laws governing social discipline, such as penalties for drunkenness and adultery, and introduced social, economic and political reforms to strengthen Aztec rule. These measures are known from indigenous chronicles preserved after the conquest. He is often confused with his descendant [[Moctezuma II|Moctezuma II]].

Value that occurs most often in a data set or probability distribution. The mode is one of three main measures of central tendency, along with the [[Median|median]] and mean. For a discrete [[Random variable|random variable]] it is the value with the highest probability. A data set may be unimodal (one mode), bimodal or multimodal, or amodal if all values occur equally often. In the set {1, 2, 2, 3, 4}, the mode is 2. Because it can be applied to nominal and categorical data, where arithmetic operations do not apply, the mode is widely used in fields such as epidemiology and market research. In a symmetric unimodal distribution such as the [[Normal distribution|normal distribution]], the mean, median and mode coincide.

Non-human species or strain studied intensively to reveal biological principles that apply to other organisms. Model organisms are chosen for traits such as short generation times, small size, ease of cultivation and well-characterized genomes. They allow research into human disease when experiments on people would be unfeasible or unethical, because living things share common descent and conserved pathways. Common examples include *Escherichia coli*, [[Yeast|baker's yeast]], *Drosophila melanogaster*, *Caenorhabditis elegans* and the mouse. Thomas Hunt Morgan's work with *Drosophila* from 1910 to 1927 showed that chromosomes carry genes. Animal research contributed to the 1922 discovery of [[Insulin|insulin]] and to the near-eradication of [[Polio|polio]]. Animal models have poor predictive accuracy for clinical toxicity and efficacy, and their use remains ethically contested.

Person hired to display products, especially clothing, or to pose for an artist. Modeling uses the body to represent another body or an artist's imagination, and differs from acting or dancing in that personal opinions are normally not expressed. Types include fine art, [[Fashion|fashion]], glamour, fitness and body-part modeling, and models appear in magazines, films, television and online media. The profession grew with fashion magazines and photography in the early 20th century, and the first modeling agencies were founded in the 1920s. Studies report disordered eating among 20–40% of models, compared with lower rates in the general population, which is linked to mandates for thinness. Historical underrepresentation of non-white models in top bookings is also cited as a concern.

Any of a group of malleable substances used for sculpting and building three-dimensional forms. Modeling clays vary widely in composition. Oil-based clays such as Plasticine combine kaolinite, [[Gypsum|gypsum]] and oils or waxes to stay soft and reusable. Plasticine was developed in 1897 by the English art teacher William Harbutt in Bath, England, as a reusable alternative to clays that harden and crack. Polymer clays harden when baked, air-hardening clays dry without heat, and [[Ceramic|ceramic]] clays require firing in a kiln. Paper clays contain fibers for lightweight models. Modeling clay is widely used in art education and stop-motion animation, as in *Wallace & Gromit*. Some polymer clays contain phthalates, so care is advised.
